I recently wore this to one of my kid’s theater performances and heard “Oh my god, I love your jacket!” so many times. — Julie Sprankles

I love dangly earrings, but they can be uncomfortable or look *too* fancy. These lovely guys are 18k gold-plated recycled sterling silver with Cubic Zirconia Stones and retail for under $100 — and they come in the cutest holiday packaging. — Sarah Aswell

I’ve long believed that a good pair of boots can make any woman feel like a total put-together badass, but I’m over 40 now... boots can’t just be aesthetic; they also have to be comfortable. I love how it goes with everything, and I can't leave the house without people complimenting it. #8026. Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

The videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”

Simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It says just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

We caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

Probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to plan, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

We are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

In repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

What do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an important thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

There's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?"

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?"

#8025. Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 12, 2026

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global company has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that showed Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most important thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology company behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

Alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most important pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really important. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

Alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a plan in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

Alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

#8023. 46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.)

Since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

Basically, it’s a big ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

This is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

These cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

In the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

The Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity

My 15-year-old and I are both big Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles

Seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that says “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity

I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles

Practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta

Sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this new classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell

This sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity

This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles

I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta

This is a new brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity

Both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles

I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta

My 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell

For the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity

If your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles

I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta

This brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell

Cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity

These I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles

My kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell

If your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity

I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles

My daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell

Buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity

These M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles

The problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell

For the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a big gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity

I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles

All my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity

For years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell

I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a new driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles

I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity

My artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles

For the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity

This is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this company has been really great for us. I also love that this comes in a sturdy carrying case and with a swatch card, which my daughter loves to fill out as soon as she gets a new set. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who's obsessed with her dog (or everyone else's), this dog-themed earring set from Pip Pop Post is a super cute way to show it off. The earrings are made from hypoallergenic 18k gold-plated stainless steel with colorful enamel, and they're free of nickel, lead, and copper, so they're comfortable for sensitive ears. They use flat screw-back posts that stay put through sleep, sports, and school, and they're waterproof and sweat-proof, so she can wear them 24/7 without a second thought! — Katie Garrity

Every year, we get the kids a holiday-themed puzzle from Mudpuppy. The quality is great, and the puzzles are challenging without being a nightmare. Many of them have foil details, which make them so pretty and fun. Especially as my kids get older and there are fewer traditional toys under the tree, having a puzzle to settle around on Christmas afternoon while we watch 'Miracle on 34th Street 'is a real crowd-pleaser. — Sarah Aswell

If you were a kid in the ‘90s like I was, you probably remember the absolute thrill of a fresh pack of Gelly Roll pens. Well, I’m happy to report they’re still just as magical for tweens and teens today! This 74-pen gift set from Sakura has every color imaginable, from metallics to bright neons, and I know my artsy teen is going to flip when they find it under the tree. The pens are perfect for doodling, coloring, junk journaling, or even just making handmade cards for friends (one of my teen’s favorite hobbies). And, yes, I’ll obviously be borrowing a few for my own desk. — Julie Sprankles

#8021. Your kid needs you to have hobbies outside of motherhood. Here’s why

Hobbies aren’t a luxury for moms. They boost well-being, nurture identity, and show our children what a full life looks like.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 13, 2026

Twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

When I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly said, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”

Like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

“A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” says Carly Snyder, a New York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”

In an effort to start prioritizing my own interests, I jumped at the chance to sign up for a summer swim league for adults aptly named “Grown-Up Swimming.” The whole experience reignited my love for swimming, and it showed me and my kids that I’m more than just a mom.

Research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

Hobbies offer a particularly important lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington says. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

One day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington says. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

No longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she says. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”

Science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder says. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”

Snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she says. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder says. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”

It’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”

Your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder says.

Search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

When you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

“Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?

#8019. 6 Gardening Jobs You Must Finish Before the First Hard Freeze – Or You’ll Regret it in Spring

A hard freeze can do damage you won't see until spring, from cracked pots to rotten bulbs. These tasks can't wait for winter – and the window is closing fast, so hurry!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even in November, backyards can look like they got some time left, perhaps with a few late-season tomatoes still clinging to the vine and container tropicals green on the patio. But all it takes is one hard freeze, dropping overnight temperatures with a day or two’s notice. Suddenly, tender leaves turn black and crops are ruined. What’s worse is that much of the damage stays hidden until spring.

You’ll only discover a split copper pipe when you turn on the hose in April, or realize you lost your prized dahlia tubers when green shoots fail to emerge. Sure, not every chore needs to be tackled now. Routine pruning and bed edging can wait until late winter. However, certain tasks carry a hard deadline set by the weather: this includes anything involving overwintering plants, as well as plumbing fixtures that hold water.

In some yards, this deadline has already passed, and in others, it's coming up this week. Completing the following tasks before temperatures plunge can save you hundreds of dollars in expensive winter damage, and keeps everything in the best shape for spring. Here’s how to make sure your garden emerges strong and healthy next year.

Understanding the difference between a light frost and a hard freeze can give you the lead time you need. Growers sometimes talk about frosts and freezes interchangeably, but the differences matter. A light frost occurs when air temperatures hover right at the freezing threshold (32°F / 0°C), forming ice crystals on leaf surfaces. While tender annuals like basil and coleus blacken quickly at this temperature, cold-tolerant vegetables like kale shrug it off (and even taste better).

A hard freeze is more aggressive. It occurs when ambient temperatures drop to 28°F (-2°C) or lower and remain there for several hours. At this depth of cold, ice crystals form inside plant cell walls, bursting cellular membranes and killing unhardened woody stems. A hard freeze also freezes water inside pipes, outdoor faucets, and irrigation lines. True frozen ground, where soil hardens into an impenetrable crust, usually develops weeks later after sustained sub-freezing weather.

Northern gardens are often done by November, while milder regions may still have several weeks. Because first-freeze dates are geographical moving targets, your regional location dictates your timeline. Gardeners in northern USDA hardiness zones 3-5 often face hard freezes by mid-October, while those in milder zones 7-9 may not see temperatures dip below 28°F until late December or January. This can help prevent panicking too early – or waiting too late.

Don’t wait for a freeze warning to assemble your gear. Keeping insulated spigot covers, garden forks, frost fabric, and storage crates on hand now ensures you can secure your yard quickly when the first blue whistler rolls in. To help you track things, it’s also a good idea to have a thermometer on standby. The TempPro TempAir 500 FT Indoor/Outdoor Thermometer, available from Amazon, can help you to stay one step ahead of any overnight shocks. Then you’re ready to tackle these tasks…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One frost can ruin tomatoes, peppers, eggplants, and basil. Even near-freezing temperatures in the mid-30s can cause chilling injury to peppers and eggplants, dulling skin quality and introducing rot spots. So strip your vines of all mature crops before freezing weather arrives. Use sharp scissors or snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Garden Snips from Amazon.

Gather every ripe tomato, along with full-sized green tomatoes that have developed a glossy, pale-green sheen. Placed in a cardboard box indoors at room temperature, mature green fruits will ripen off the vine over the next few weeks. Leave small, hard fruits behind, as they lack the maturity to ripen. Pull up basil plants to process into pesto or dry indoors.

However, you can leave cool-season brassicas and root crops where they are. Collards, Brussels sprouts, kale, carrots, and parsnips tolerate temperatures well below 28°F (-2°C). The cold triggers these hardy crops to convert complex starches into plant sugars, which can help them taste sweeter after frost.

In regions with cold winters (typically zones 7 and colder), tender summer-flowering bulbs, tubers, and corms won’t survive in freezing ground. Leaving dahlias, cannas, calla lilies, caladiums, gladioli, and tuberous begonias in the soil too long, and the fleshy storage organs will freeze, decompose, and turn to mush. Dahlias and cannas benefit from waiting until an initial light frost blackens the foliage. (Tuberous begonias are more tender and often need to get lifted earlier as the leaves yellow.)

Once that light freeze hits, don’t wait for the ground to freeze solid. Cut black stems back to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). Carefully insert a garden fork into the earth, at least 12 inches (30cm) from the main stalk to avoid impaling the tubers. Gently pry the root clump upward. Shake off loose soil, and allow the tubers to cure in a dry, frost-free garage for a few days.

Then gently pack in cardboard boxes filled with dry peat moss, vermiculite, or wood shavings. You can buy Plantonix Premium Vermiculite Bliss from Walmart to help protect dahlia and canna tubers against humidity spikes and fungal rots. Store in a dark, cool space between 40-50°F (4-10°C). Where winters are mild (zone 8 and warmer), dahlias can stay in the ground, provided soil drains freely and is protected with mulch.

Plumbing and outdoor water features carry the highest financial risk when a hard freeze arrives. Water expands by about 9% when it turns to ice. Even if your home features modern "frost-free" outdoor hose spigots, leaving a garden hose attached prevents the internal valve from draining properly. The pipe inside the wall can split, unnoticed until it leaks in spring. So uncouple every hose, stretch them out on a gentle incline to drain residual water, and roll them up for indoor storage.

If your home has an interior shutoff valve for exterior spigots, close it now. Open the outside tap to bleed the line, and then secure an insulated foam faucet cover over the fixture. You can get Frost King FC1 Foam Faucet Covers from Walmart in double packs. Drip lines can usually be drained by opening the end caps. In-ground lawn sprinkler systems require compressed air to blow all standing water out of the pipes, manifold valves, and pop-up heads. Too much air pressure can crack pipes and heads, so if you don't know your system, winterizing sprinklers is better left to a pro.

Anything holding standing water is at risk. Drain cast concrete, ceramic, and stone water fountains. Cover them with waterproof tarps to prevent pooled water from freezing and cracking the masonry. For bird baths, stone bowls will split under hard freezes, so store decorative basins indoors. To support backyard birds in winter, add a designated heated bird bath such as the Gesail Heated Bird Bath from Amazon. You can attach this to a decking or balcony and it’s a great depth for smaller songbirds. Alternatively, float a clean rubber ball or rubber duck on the surface of frost-safe metal basins to keep surface water moving.

Container-grown plants are far more vulnerable to cold than specimens planted in garden beds. Cold air surrounds the container on all sides, dropping potting soil temperatures up to 20°F lower than garden beds. An outdoor shrub rated hardy to your zone might still freeze and die if left unprotected in a pot. Roots in a pot sit above ground, with cold reaching them from the sides as well as the top. They're also less cold-hardy than the stems above them.

Tropical plants, potted citrus, pelargoniums, and tender patio perennials should be moved indoors once nighttime temperatures hover around 50°F (10°C). Before anything goes inside, inspect leaf undersides and stem junctions for hitchhiking pests like aphids, mealybugs, and spider mites, as well as webs or anything sticky. Wash the foliage with a gentle stream of water. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to roll heavy container citrus plants and tropicals indoors. Keep them apart from houseplants until you're sure nothing hitched a ride.

Pots left out need plants rated a zone or two hardier than your area. For hardy perennials, boxwoods, and dwarf conifers in large patio containers, group pots along a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall. Elevate on pot feet to ensure drainage holes remain ice-free, and wrap in burlap or bubble wrap to protect root balls from freezing solid. An unheated garage is fine for many hardy potted plants: just water them now and then so the soil doesn't dry out completely.

Fall is an ideal time for planting perennials and shrubs, but specimens tucked into borders within the last 6-8 weeks have not had long to root and establish. As freeze-thaw cycles strike, frost heave can push shallow perennial crowns and strawberry plants out of the ground. Mulch can help, but you need to time this right. Wait until after the first hard freeze has cooled the ground.

Once the top inch of soil is cold, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose organic mulch to new plantings and strawberry patches. Good options are shredded pine bark, clean wheat straw, or chopped leaves. You can buy Timberline Pine Bark Nuggets from The Home Depot. Keep it pulled back 2-3 inches (5-8cm) from plant crowns to prevent moisture buildup and winter rot.

Vulnerable shrubs require above-ground shielding. Broadleaf evergreens like boxwood, rhododendron, and cherry laurel continue to lose moisture through their leaves in winter. Combined with winter sun and wind, this can cause foliage burn. Water deeply before soil freezes. Then drive stakes into the ground around vulnerable shrubs while the soil is still workable, and fasten some burlap to form a windbreak. On old-wood bigleaf hydrangeas, use these screens to protect fragile flower buds.

Porous containers left out in freezing conditions are a common source of costly winter loss. Unglazed terracotta, ceramic pots, and composite clay planters absorb water during fall rains. When temperatures plunge below 28°F (-2°C), the moisture trapped within the clay walls expands, causing pottery to crack and split. This won’t always be obvious until spring, when a planter crumbles as soon as it is lifted.

Before freezing weather arrives, empty all unused potting soil, as a damp potting mix retains water that accelerates cracking. Scrub the inside walls with a stiff brush to remove mineral salts. For a good set of stiff bristles, buy the OXO Good Grips Heavy Duty Scrub Brush from Amazon. Allow the pottery to dry in the sun, then store the containers upside down in an unheated shed, garage, or dry basement. If planters are too heavy to move inside, empty the soil, turn them upside down on wooden blocks off the ground, and secure a waterproof tarp over them.

Take a few minutes to drain all watering cans, sprayers, and outdoor hoses, storing them where residual water cannot freeze and split their seams. Finish by scraping dried soil off spades, trowels, and hoes. Wipe the blades with a rag dipped in mineral or vegetable oil. This will prevent rust while tools sit idle over the winter months.

Some common fall chores can wait until well after the first hard freeze. In fact, tackling certain jobs too early can do more harm than good. Hold off pruning deciduous shade trees, fruit trees, and summer-blooming shrubs like panicle hydrangeas until late winter or early spring. Pruning now opens fresh wounds that cannot form protective callus tissue before a severe cold sets in, increasing the risk of injury and infection.

General border clean-up and leaf raking can also be paced out. Leaving dried flower heads, ornamental grasses, and hollow perennial stems standing in early winter provides structural interest in snowy beds. More importantly, these standing seed heads supply winter food for foraging birds like goldfinches, while hollow stems provide shelter for overwintering native bees and beneficial insects.

Finally, mulching hybrid tea roses and established perennial crowns can wait until several hard freezes have pushed plants into deep dormancy and chilled the soil. Rushing to mulch warm soil traps ground heat, delaying dormancy and encouraging tender shoots. Focus your immediate energy on plumbing, tender crops, and cold-vulnerable tubers; the rest can be tidied over the coming weekends.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8018. I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

When my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

By tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

Then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

The nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

#8017. Max Greenfield Is That Dad

In a new film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.

The first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect. That’s only the start of the aspirational cues coming from this character played by Max Greenfield. In this funny — and, yes, tear-jerking — family drama, Greenfield’s character juggles work, elementary-aged twins, a big-feeling teen, and his wife’s cancer diagnosis. While he is at times off-kilter from all that life throws his way in the film, this dad does not bumble his way through it. In every scene, he finds ways to be the emotionally available parent and partner.

Greenfield says that understanding the character was easy. “There’s so much of me that’s in that movie,” he tells Fatherly. “I felt so close to what we were doing.” It could be, perhaps, because his daughter, like the main character, is a high schooler; she has mutual friends to the lead actress, Sunny Sandler; and her experience — at least onstage, navigating high school life — just resonated.

We sat down to give Max Greenfield the Cool Dad questionnaire, and then talked about the movie, finding patience, and fighting parental anxiety — and why LA’s bagels are seriously underrated.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

I finished watching Don’t Say Good Luck today. I definitely did some crying.

They keep playing clips in these interviews that I’m doing for press, and they’ll play it before the interview, and I’m constantly like, “I need a minute.”

It’s intense. It’s a wonderful film. I’m wondering how close of a dad are you to who you play on screen in Don’t Say Good Luck. Are you that dad?

I mean, there’s so much of me that’s in that movie. I felt so close to what we were doing. It was really the reason I wanted to do it. My daughter, I think, is a year younger than Sunny [Sandler, the lead], and I was really aware that this was going to be a movie that Sunny was starring in. And from everything that I had heard, I had never done a Sandler movie before, but his sets are famously the best. And so I really wanted to just make sure that she had a comparable experience on this with somebody else. I felt like I knew how to do that.

My daughter and her have mutual friends, I know where she goes to school… just a lot of the stuff I just was like, “I know this world well.” And so talking to somebody like Sunny is not an issue for me. And trying to be light and supportive in this environment, it was something I felt like I was capable of doing. I didn’t know if I was going to be very good in the movie as an actor, but I was like, “I think I know how to be the dad.” And then there’s the two young boys in the movie, the twins, and they were so funny because they were just never acting. They just were running around.

They’re a little bit younger than my son, but I just coached my son’s basketball team, and wrangling all those kids and getting them going, getting them involved, it was very good prep work for dealing with these two boys. And it made the scenes and made the movie so much fun.

Yeah. Everything was just like, “Oh, this is what my real life is.” And being there with Sunny, I understood that relationship. Being there with the boys, I was like, “I get this relationship.”

There was a more dramatically real scene later in the movie … I personally had a similar experience to the lead character. My mom had cancer when I was a sophomore in high school, and all I could think about was how I wanted you — your character — to be my dad for that time. For example, that scene when you were sitting in the car and Sunny asked, “Are you okay?” And you asked, “Are you okay?” And both of you said, “No.” It was just… right.

That was a really cool scene. Julia Hart, who had directed the movie and wrote the movie along with Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz … [had] a lot of conversations about that scene, and they were so generous in my input. It really felt like that scene was going to be the scene for this relationship. And as we started to see how the movie was playing out and what was happening before then, we had sent a bunch of drafts of that scene back and forth to one another, and we all collectively landed in that spot because it really needed to set up everything that comes after that, but it needed to honor everything that was built up before it, and it needed to feel real.

I didn’t want there to be an answer or a fix to what was happening, but I wanted them to feel it, both characters. When we shot that scene, it was nuts. It was really heavy, man.

In this movie, you run a bagel shop. So what’s your order?

Oh, wow. Great question. I’ve probably gotten older and more healthy than I need to be, more LA than I need to be. I’ll give you two. One’s an everything bagel [with] just cream cheese, onion, tomato, lox.

That can’t ever miss, it’s the best. The other one is … either a light cream cheese spread [or] the right type of hummus and then just veggies. But fresh, good veggies that are with the right type of dressing on it and salt and pepper. There’s a place in LA that has been hyped and hyped and I finally went there, I don’t know, a month or two ago. It’s called Courage Bagels. And the line is a mile long. And I was like, “I’m not waiting in line.” And then my daughter and I were like, “Let’s go wait in line.” So we went over there and they had one, I think it’s called the Garden or something. I don’t know. Holy sh*t. It was unbelievable.

One of the big themes of the movie I wanted to get your take on is disclosure to children. That is, what you tell a kid, what you don’t tell a kid, when you’re protecting them from the truth, and when that backfires. I was just wondering if you had thoughts on how you strike that personally.

It’s a really good question. I actually feel like I’ve done a good job with this, personally. There are certain things that I want them to discover on their own, and hopefully my job is to have created a space where they feel comfortable to then bring those things up to me. And then depending on how the question’s asked or how much they want to know, you ease them into certain topics of discussion and what you choose to discover based on what they’re asking. And you let that conversation be ongoing. And so I’ve had some real good success in some areas where those conversations have opened up and become more in-depth over time. And as a result, I see that my kids are way more comfortable with information that I was worried might be confusing or scary. And because they’ve sort of been able to take it in at their pace.

How has your outlook changed now that you’re past the baby and elementary parenting and you have a 16- and 11-year-old?

I’m making a lot more mistakes. That thing we talked about, responsibility versus what to let go, that line is thinner and thinner every day. And there’s so many times where, what are the things that I feel like I need to control to make me feel safer in this situation that is so scary? And being a fear-based parent is not a good zone to operate from.

And so it’s like my daughter’s now driving and she gets her driver’s license and it’s just like, my wife and I are both like, “Well, so the next day, is she just driving to volleyball practice? Is that how that works?” And if you strip all the fear away from it, you’re like, “Yeah, she practiced and worked up to it and has now passed the test and she’s allowed to legally drive. So yes, why wouldn’t she be able to?” There’s a period of time when they’re small where you’re like, “Yeah, this is just going to keep getting better.” And then it shifts in the most terrifying way and you’re like, “Oh, this is all so much worse.”

When we were [learning to drive], I would sit in the car with her, we would drive, and I would go, “Oh, you know what? All the anxiety and fear I have about the future and life and work and all the nonsense, that’s not real.” When I’m sitting in a car with my daughter and she’s driving, this is real fear. This is what real fear feels like. It’s like, this is the shark in the water kind of fear. And it’s heavy and it’s tangible. And you almost hold it and you go, “This is what real fear feels like, and this is appropriate for the situation.” So outside of that, when I do feel any sort of anxiety about the future or whatever it is, I go, “Oh, this is not real.” And now I know the difference. So at least I have that.
